text: An EC2 instance type name like m5.large or c6g.xlarge isn't arbitrary — it's structured. The family letter tells you what the hardware is optimized for, the generation number tells you which generation of AWS hardware, an optional capability letter flags something like a Graviton or AMD processor, and the size tells you how much of that profile you actually get.

describe-instance-types is how you confirm the real numbers instead of guessing. Filter by a family prefix like m5, and it returns the actual vCPU count and memory in MiB for every matching type currently offered — faster and more current than memorizing specs that change every time AWS ships a new generation of hardware. Run it before you commit a production launch to a type you've only seen mentioned in a blog post.

Take c6g.xlarge apart piece by piece: c means compute-optimized, 6 is the generation, g means it runs on AWS Graviton ARM processors instead of Intel, and xlarge is the size — doubling the size roughly doubles the vCPU and memory you get. Once you can read one name this way, you can read any instance type on sight.

Four families cover most decisions. T-series is burstable — baseline CPU plus credits you spend to burst above it, perfect for low, spiky load, but it throttles under sustained demand. M-series is balanced general purpose with steady performance and no bursting — the default for production app servers. C-series is compute-optimized, for CPU-bound work like batch jobs and video encoding. R-series is memory-optimized, for in-memory caches and large databases where the working set needs to fit in RAM.

Picking the wrong family either wastes money on headroom you'll never use, or throttles a workload that needed sustained CPU all along — the family letter is a hardware promise, not a habit.
